# Native aggregates, tagged values and pattern expressions (SIM-007)

The task module runs every positive fixture through the public CLI in both HDL
optimizer modes on legacy, compact/portable and compact/GMP values, and after the frontend snapshot and owned Db are
destroyed. Expected outputs are derived by hand from the cited clauses, not
captured from llg.

A one-dimensional fixed unpacked array whose elements are strings, identity
handles or records with string, real or handle members is stored as a fixed
array view of the recursive container runtime: each element is one owned
value, a runtime select reads or writes it in place, and copies are deep
except for handles (SV 7.4, 7.6, 8.4).

| Fixture | Clause and independent oracle |
| --- | --- |
| `native_arrays` | IEEE 1800-2009 §§7.4, 7.4.6, 7.6, 10.4.2, 10.9, 11.4.5, 11.4.11, 13.4. (1) Elements start as empty strings; `$size` is 3. (2) Positional patterns fill in declaration order: `up[1..3]` = a b c, `dn[3..1]` = x y z. (3-6) `always_comb` follows the runtime select `up[k]`: a, then c for k = 3, then C after `up[3] = "C"`, then the empty string for the out-of-range k = 7 (§7.4.6, no warning). (7, 8) Index keys name declared indices and `default` fills the rest: `d two d`; `three ? one`. (9) `'{3{"r"}}` replicates: rrr. (10) The reversing pattern reads every source before writing: rqp. (11) `dn = up` copies by position (dn[3] = up[1]) and stays independent of a later write: `rqp R`. (12) `cp == dn` compares element by element in storage order (r q p both): 1, 0; `cp === up` sees `r` against `R`: 0, 1. (13) `cp[0:1] = dn[2:1]` copies q p: qpp. (14) `cp[k+:2]` with k = 1 takes `up[1:2]` = R q: qRq. (15, 16) A known condition selects one arm: ttt, then `up` = Rqp. (17) An unknown condition keeps equal elements and gives the empty string elsewhere: `[R][][p]`. (18-20) Calls copy the array in and out: `R--p`; `fill` writes z, zz, zzz; a pattern actual is built before the display: `m-n-o`. (21) `rb = ra` copies the records; renaming `rb[0].s` leaves `ra[0]`: `one uno 2 2.5`. (22) `ra == rb` is 0 (one string differs), `!=` 1. (23) `'{default: rec_t'{...}}` fills both records: `9 nine 9 nine`. (24) `swap_pick(ra, 0)` returns `ra[1]` through its swapped local copy: `2 two 2.5`. (25) Nonblocking writes use issue-time values: `up[1]` becomes N1, `up[2]` the old `up[1]` (R), and `rb <= ra` copies record 0 (`1 one`). |
| `handle_records` | §§7.2, 8.4, 13.4, 13.5. Copying a record copies its class handle, so `bump` changes the shared object: `a a+ 11 11 1`. A record element of a fixed array is passed by value and the result stored in another element: `a++ 12 0.25`. An `inout` record formal copies back into an element: `z a+`. Rebinding `b.h` leaves `a.h` at 12; a never-set element handle is null: `12 1 1`. Assigning `a` into `list[0]` shares the object, so writing 99 through the element is seen through `a.h`: 99. |
| `native_tagged` | §§7.3.2, 11.9, 12.6, 12.6.1, 12.6.2. A tagged union with string, real, record, class-handle and packed members keeps the tag and each member separately. (1) `tagged I 5` reads 5. (2) `x.S` is appended to while S is active and `y = x` copies it (`str!`); `x` then holds F = 2.5. (3) `y matches tagged S .s` binds `str!`; (4) `x` holds F, so the S test fails. (5) `tagged F .r &&& r > 2.0` binds 2.5 and prints 5.0. (6) The record member is assigned by a pattern and updated in place: `rec 8`; (7) `tagged Rec .*` matches. (8) A handle member shares its object: 30 written through `x.H` is read through `b`. (9) `tagged B 8'h5a` matches exactly; (10) the binding `.k` with filter `k[0] == 0` prints `5a`. (11) In plain `case`, `?` digits are literal Z bits, so `8'b0101????` does not match `5a`: default; (12) `casez` treats them as wildcards: matches. (13) `tagged None` selects the void item. (14) A binding in a case item feeds its `&&&` filter: `case`. |
| `native_tagged_inactive` | §§7.3.2, 11.9. Every inactive access reports `access to inactive tagged-union member` with its source location and run-time failure (exit 1; the reports go to stderr and the `$display` lines to stdout): (1) the never-assigned union has no active member, so `x.S` reports and reads the empty string; (2) with I active, `x.S` and `x.F` report and read `""` and 0.0; (3) the write `x.S = "lost"` reports and stores nothing, then `x.I = 9` succeeds; (4) with S active the write to I reports and `x.S` still reads `kept`. |
| `native_tagged_calls` | SIM-007-A03; §§7.3.2, 11.4.11, 12.6, 12.6.1, 13.3-13.5. A tagged union with packed, string, real, record, class-handle and void members in subroutine storage keeps the tag and each member in one native value. (1-5) `make(k)` builds each member in a local and returns it; `show` matches it with packed, string and real bindings and wildcard reads: `S s0`, `F 2.5`, `R r 3`, `H 9` (the shared object), `None`. (6) `bump` increments the record member in place: `R r 4`. (7) `bump(h)` rebuilds `tagged I 5` from the binding. (8) The static local keeps the last I value: 4 for `h`, still 4 for a string argument. (9) The timed task copies its input after `#1`, the output receives `S s0!`, the inout `h` becomes `I 5`. (10) Tagged constructions are operands of expression calls: `R p 7`, `F 0.5`. (11) The conditional operator selects an arm (`I 1`, `S x`) and keeps a member when both arms are equal under an unknown condition (`S y`); (12) a module-level conditional with `c = 0` selects `r` (`S y`). |
| `native_tagged_ports` | SIM-007-A03; §§7.3.2, 12.6, 23.3.3. The input link copies the tag and member storage and the stage matches it: `tagged I 3` doubles to 6 (no string, `n` = -1); `tagged S "four"` passes through with length 4; the record member arrives (`r 2`, -1) and a member-only write (`k` = 9) re-runs the link; the handle member names the same object (5); `tagged None` matches at the output. |
| `native_tagged_inactive_calls` | §§7.3.2, 11.4.11. Every inactive access in subroutine storage reports with its source location (exit 1): the write `v.S` while I is active stores nothing and the read yields `""`; a string binding binds `b`, and fails (`-`) for `None`; an unknown condition over differing tags leaves no member active, so `r.S` reports and reads `""`. |
| `native_tagged_arrays` | §§7.3.2, 7.4, 7.10, 11.4.5, 12.6, 12.6.1, 13.3-13.5. Fixed, queue, dynamic and associative arrays of a tagged union with void, int, string, real, record and class-handle members; each element owns its tag and members. `show` classifies with `case matches` (a tag X matches no item, so `default` gives `?`). (1) Construction into elements: I5, Shi, Rrec, H7. (2) Member writes on active members: `Rec.n` 3+1 = 4, `H.v = 8` changes the shared object `b` (8), `arr[0].I + 1` = 6, `S` appends `!`. (3) `v = arr[1]` and `arr[0] = v` copy whole elements; `v` retagged F 2.5 leaves `arr[0]` = Shi!. (4) `copy = arr` is a deep copy; retagging `copy[1]` None leaves `arr[1]` Shi!. (5-7) `matches` on elements: Rec wildcard, S binding with a filter (`hi!`), I against an S element fails. (8) Equality compares tags and the active member only (stale I 3 in `v` and I 4 in `arr[0]` are not compared): `v == w` 1, `arr[0] == v` 1, `arr[0] != arr[1]` ("x" vs "hi!") 1, S against H 0. (9) A pattern fills a queue: 1 a 0.5, size 3. (10) `push_back(arr[2])`, `push_front(make(-1))` and `insert(1, v)` give Sneg Sx I1 Sa F0.5 Rrec. (11) `pop_back` returns Rrec and leaves 5. (12) An output formal stores I7 into `q[1]`, an inout formal increments it to I8; `pick(q, 4)` returns F0.5. (13) `delete(0)` leaves 4 elements starting with I8. (14) `new[3]` elements have tag X (`?`), `d[1] = make(9)` is I9; `d[0] == d[2]` compares X tags: x. (15) String keys: Sax, `a["x"].S` = ax, `a["y"]` copies I8, 2 entries. (16) A run-time index `q[3]` binds F 0.5 with a filter: 0.50. (17) `case matches` on `q[2]` (Sa): a. (18) A fixed-array result reverses `fa`: r l; `fa == fb` 0, `fb != fa` 1. (19) `foreach` with `matches`: 0 l, 1 r. (20) A class queue property of the union: cls. (21) Run-time index writes I0..I30: 30 10. (22) A tagged expression resets the inactive members, so `v` (I 3, then S x) copied into `fa[0]` equals `fb[0]`, and the whole arrays compare equal element by element: 1 1. |
| `native_tagged_array_inactive` | §§7.3.2, 11.9. Inactive accesses to elements report like scalars (exit 1) with the access's source location: line 13 col 28 (`arr[0].S` while I is active), line 14 col 9 (write of `S`, nothing stored), line 15 cols 48 and 58 (`arr[1]` was never assigned, so its tag is X and both S and F are inactive), line 17 col 9 (write of `q[0].I` while S is active), line 19 col 38 (`a[4].I` while F is active). Reads yield the default: `[]`, `0.0`, and X for the four-state packed read (`x`, the same as a scalar variable); the active reads give 5 and `x` (the string stored by `push_back`). |
| `bad_tagged_element_side_effect`, `bad_tagged_nested_member`, `bad_tagged_nested_element` | A checked element access re-reads the element's tag and member in place, so a side-effecting index rejects; a tagged union with native members nested in a record (module record or queue element type) rejects, since member accesses below the record would have no tag check. |
| `native_tagged_nba`, `bad_tagged_member_nba` | §§7.3.2, 9.4.2, 10.4.2; Q03. Whole-union nonblocking writes fix the value at issue and commit the member, the reset of inactive members and the tag together. (1) Before the commit `v` is still I 1. (2) `src` changes after issue: first. (3) `w` is retagged after `v <= w`: 2.5. (4) Of two NBAs in one step the later (I 9) wins. (5) A handle member shares `b`: 3. (6) A call result: call. (7) A fixed-array element: e. (8) `v <= w; w <= v` swaps: x 1. (9, 10) A clocked pipeline `p1 <= tagged I cnt; p2 <= p1` over three edges with `cnt` 0, 1, 2: `p2` = 1, `p1` = 2. A member write `v.S <= "b"` must be checked against the tag at commit (SV 11.9, Q03); queued native writes have no such check, so it is rejected. |
| `native_record_selects` | §§7.2, 7.4, 10.9, 12.5, 13.4.1. (1) `case (s)` on a module string compares strings: B. (2) `zz` matches no item: default. (3) `unique case` on a concatenated string: zz!. (4) A function's string case: first, second, other. (5) Members of a record array inside a native record: `m.fa[1]` = 4 z, `m.fa[0].a` = 5, `m.fa[0].t` empty. (6) A nested record pattern item from a call: in 3 2, one call. (7) The pattern reads `o` before writing: `k` = 3, inner = f("in+", 2): in+ 2 3, two calls. (8) Members of call results: `f("x", 5).s` = x, `f("y", 6).n + 1` = 7, four calls. (9) Call-result members in a condition, both evaluated: 6 calls. Class properties of record type are SIM-011 (`sim_011/record_properties`). |
| `witness_tagged_native`, `witness_string_binding`, `witness_string_array_pattern`, `witness_record_slice`, `witness_string_array_return` | Adopted FND-002 witnesses (ledger L-F02-09-01/L-F05-08-03 `tagged_native`, L-F05-08-02 `native_pattern_match`, L-F05-05-02 `native_array_pattern`, and the SIM-003 child items `record_slice` and `string_array_return`); each expected line is the witness's `Expected:` header; the copies end with a quiet `$finish(0)`. |
| `native_member_select` | §§7.4.6, 13.5. Run-time indices into member arrays of a module record and of a record formal. (1) `k = 1` reads `b`, `a[2] = 7`, `r[1] = 1.5`. (2) Writes through `k` set `s[1] = B`, `a[1] = 5`. (3) `k = 9` is out of range: reads give `""`, 0 and 0.0; (4) the writes store nothing, so the record is unchanged (`aBc`, `0 5 7 0`). (5) An X index (`logic` variable) reads the defaults. (6) The formal copy of `n` is edited at index 1 (`xwz/w`); index 2 reads `z`; index -1 reads `""`; (7) `n` itself is unchanged. (8) Editing the copy of `m` at index 2 gives `aBw/w`. (9) Packed member selects: `p = 5a`, `p[3:0] = c` gives `5c`, `p[7] = 1` gives `dc`; `p[7:4]` is `d` and `p[1]` is 0. |
| `native_member_select_wide` | §§7.2, 7.4.5, 7.4.6 L8235 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`). Run-time indices into string, real, handle, record and packed member arrays of 65 to 70 elements, descending and negative bounds included, on a module record and a record formal. An invalid or X index reads the default and writes nothing (S07-D1 applies the same rule; some simulators stop). Nonblocking writes choose the element at issue (§10.4.2 L13070-13072): `i = 3` in a later region does not move them, untimed writes commit in the step's NBA region and `#2` ones two steps later. The lines before the invalid-index section were confirmed on an industry-standard simulator. |
| `native_member_select_index_forms` | §§7.4.5, 7.4.6 L8235 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`). The index's value decides, with its own signedness and whole width, in a chain (`c`, 3 elements) and a tree (`t`, `n`, `[-2:9]`): signed byte -2 and `longint` -2 select `t[-2]`; unsigned byte 9 selects `t[9]`; `8'hfe` is 254, not -2, and all-ones `logic [63:0]` is not -1, so both are invalid; a 65-bit index with bit 64 set and low bits 3 is invalid, 65-bit 3 selects `t[3]`, signed 65-bit -1 selects `t[-1]`; -3 and 10 are out of range; X and Z bits are invalid; an expression index `k + 1` selects `t[2]`. Invalid reads give `""` and 0, invalid writes store nothing. `always_comb` over `r.n[idx]` follows the index and the selected element. The valid-index lines were confirmed on an industry-standard simulator, except the last selected-element line. Some simulators stop at an invalid index (S07-D1). Some keep only the low 32 bits of an index, so 65-bit bit 64 plus 3 selects `t[3]` and all-ones selects `t[-1]`; §7.4.6 L8235 ("If an index expression is out of the address bounds or if any bit in the address is X or Z, then the index shall be invalid") decides here. Some do not rerun the `always_comb` after `r.n[5] = 55` (stale 50); §9.2.2.2.1 L11184 ("The implicit sensitivity list of an always_comb includes the expansions of the longest static prefix of each") decides here, so 55. |
| `bad_member_select_limit` | A member array of 4,097 strings is above the dense record threshold of 4,096 elements, so the module record itself is rejected at code generation with the bound in the message. |
| `record_element_equality` | §§7.2, 11.4.5. Whole record elements of queues, dynamic and associative arrays compare member-wise against each other and module records. (1) `q[0]` and `p[0]` hold equal members: 1; `q[1]` differs from `p[0]`: 0; `!=` gives 0; `q[1] == m`: 1. (2) `m == q[1]` and `d[1] == q[1]` (both copies of `m`): 1; the default `d[0]` differs from `q[0]`: 0. (3) `a["x"]` is a copy of `m`: equal to `d[1]`, not to `d[0]`. (4) `k = 7` is past the queue end, so `q[7]` reads the default: equal to `d[0]`, unequal to `p[0]`. (5) After `q[0].s = "A"` the string member differs: 0; the member reads `A`: 1. (6) `4'b10x1` members: `===` matches the X exactly (1, `!==` 0) while `==` is unknown (`x`). |
| `native_patterns` | §§10.9, 10.9.1, 10.9.2. (1) `'{string: "st", default: 0}` sets both strings and leaves `i`, `r` at 0. (2) The member key `t` wins over the `string` type key, `int` sets 4 and `default` fills the real: `4 st tt 1.5`. (3) An index key with `default` on a string array: `d x d`. (4) Nested type keys and a replicated string pair: `2 q q 0.5 w w`. (5) `'{2{rec}}` gives two independent copies: renaming `ra[0].s` leaves `ra[1].s` at `a`. (6) A pattern reading its own destination swaps `s`/`t` (old values `st`/`tt`) and an independent target copies the same sources with `i + 1`. (7) `ra = '{ra[1], ra[0]}` swaps records: `a A`. (8) Rotating a string array reads every old element (`d x d` becomes `d d x`). (9) A nested record and its member array exchange values through one pattern: `x.s` gets `u[0]` (w), `x.t` the old `x.s` (q), `u[0]` the old `x.t` (q). (10) Handle members swap identities and the string member reads its old value: after swapping, `p.b` is the object created with 1; setting `p.b.v = 10` leaves `p.a.v` (2): `2 10 p!`. |
| `bad_pattern_keys`, `bad_pattern_shape` | Frontend diagnostics (§§10.9.1, 10.9.2): an index key and a member key given twice; a positional pattern with three items for two elements; a real item for a string member. |
| `record_containers` | §§7.2, 7.2.2, 7.5, 7.6, 7.8, 7.10, 10.9. A queue, dynamic or associative member of a module record is its own container. (1) `'{5, 1, 3}`, `push_back(7)`, `push_front(9)` and `insert(2, 4)` give 9 5 4 1 3 7: size 6, first 9, last 7, `q[2]` = 4. (2) `pop_front` and `delete(0)` leave 4 1 3 7; `sort` gives 1 3 4 7, printed by `foreach`; the sum is 15. (3) `new[3]` and `d[2] = 8`. (4) String and integer keyed members: 2 entries, `k["two"]` = 2, `"three"` absent, `b[-3]` = 5a. (5) A member of a nested record: 11, size 1. (6) `n = m` copies the containers: later writes to `m.q[0]` and `m.d[2]` leave `n` at `m 1 4 8`. (7) `y = x` likewise: `y.k["one"]` stays 1 and `y.b` keeps its entry while `x.b` is emptied. (8) Equality is member-wise: `m.d` (0 0 0) differs from `n.d` (0 0 8): 0; after `m.d[2] = 8` both are equal (`==` 1, `!=` 0, `===` 1); one more element in `n.q`: 0. (9) Patterns build members by value: `p 2 4 8`; keyed associative items: 2 entries, `b` = 4, `b[1]` = 11. (10) A pattern copying another record's queue: `m`, `n.q[0]` = 100, `n.d` keeps 3 elements. (11) `m.q = {}` empties only `m.q`: 0 and 4. |
| `record_container_sensitivity` | §9.2.2.2. `always_comb` readers of `m.q.size()` and `m.q[0]` see the empty queue (0, -1), then the pushed 4 (1, 4), then the element write (1, 6). |
| `discarded_pops` | §§6.24.1, 7.10.2.6-7. `void'(...)` discards a popped element: `1 2 3` loses its first and last element (size 1, `2`); `0.5 1.5` loses 1.5; `a b` loses `a`; the record member `7 8` loses 7. |
| `record_container_calls` | §§7.2, 7.2.2, 7.10, 10.9, 11.4.11, 13.3-13.5. Records with queue, dynamic and associative members as subroutine formals, results and locals. (1) `make("a", 3)` builds 0 10 20 in a local and returns it: size 3, `q[2]` = 20, and `total` (an expression-call operand) sums 30. (2) The inout `grow` pushes 99 to the front and appends `+`: `a+ 99 4`. (3) The task output `fill` copies back `out` with 7 8. (4) `wrap` nests the record in a result with a dynamic member (`d[1]` = size 4) and an associative entry 5. (5) `m = a` copies; deleting `m.q[0]` leaves `a` at 4 elements, `m` at 3, unequal. (6) The static local of `counter` keeps its queue between calls: 1, 2. (7) `total(make("t", 4))` passes a call result (0+10+20+30 = 60); the static function sums `m.q` = 0 10 20: 30. (8) `build` starts from a keyed pattern (q = 1 2 3, d = 4 5, a = {k: 9}), appends 8, grows `d` to 3 keeping 4 5 and sets `d[2]` = 16, adds key `n`: `in 4 8 3 5 16 2 9 1 2.5`. (9) Equal copies compare equal (1) and the recursive `depth` appends 3, 2, 1 to its own copy: 2 + 3 = 5; after `y.q.push_back(7)`: 0, and `x` still has 2 elements. (10) The timed task copies `x` after `#1`, pushes -1 in front of its output (`later x 2 -1`), which copies back into `y`: `x 3 -1`. (11) A known-false condition selects `y` (`y 2`); an unknown one keeps only matching members, so differing names and queues give `""` and an empty queue; when both arms are equal the whole value is kept: `[x] 2 6`. |
| `record_container_ports` | §§9.2.2.2, 23.3.3. A record with a queue member through an input and an output port: the child appends the input's size (2) and renames: `a! 3 5 2`; the whole-record `@*` reader copies 2 elements and adds 1.0 to `w`; the `d.q = b.q` reader sees 3. Pushing 6 into `a.q` alone re-runs the port link, the child and both readers: `a! 4 3 3 4`. |
| `bad_record_container_element`, `bad_record_assoc_equality` | Boundaries that reject at code generation: a queue whose elements are records with an associative member (an element keeps queue and dynamic-array members as nested dynamic arrays inside its value; the runtime has no nested associative form); a nonblocking assignment of a record with a queue member (it would need issue-time copies of the member containers); equality of records with an associative member (associative-array equality is not supported). |
| `record_container_elements` | §§7.2, 7.5, 7.8, 7.10, 10.9, 11.4.5, 13.3-13.5. Records with queue, dynamic-array and string-queue members as elements of a queue, a fixed array, a dynamic array, a string-keyed associative array and a class queue property. (1) `push_back` of a variable and of a call result: 2 elements, `a`, 2 members, `list[1].q[2]` = 2; the later `r.q.push_back(9)` leaves the element alone (r has 3). (2) An element copies deeply into `r`: b, 3, 2, `d[0]` = 3/2.0 = 1.5, tag b. (3) Statements that name an element's member work on it in place: `push_back(5)` gives 1 2 5, `q[0] = 7` and `q[1]++` give 7 2 2, `push_front("t")`; sizes and values 3 5 7 2, `sum` of the element (by value) 11, t. (4) `pop_back` returns 2 and `insert(0, 3)` gives 3 7 2: 2 3 3 2. (5) `pop_front` returns a with 1 2 5, one element left. (6) `insert(0, make("c", 2))`, then `list[0] = list[1]` and `list[1].q.delete()`: b 3 0, and the elements differ (0). (7) Fixed arrays: `fixed[0] = fixed[1]` then `fixed[0].q[0] = 100`; `other = fixed` is deep, so `other[1].d[0] = 9.5` leaves `fixed[1].d[0]` = 4/2.0 = 2.0; 100 0 100 2.0 9.5, `other == fixed` 0, `fixed[0] != fixed[1]` 1. (8) A pattern of call results: p 0, q 0+1 = 1. (9) An output formal fills `dyn[0]` (out, 10 20 → 20), `dyn[1]` has 3, `count` reads `xs[0].q.size()` of the queue formal: 3. (10) A string-keyed element's member grows to 0 1 2 42: d 4 42, one entry. (11) A class's queue of such records sums `items[i].q.sum()` in a method: 3 + 4 = 7. (12) A queue pattern of a call result and a variable: 2 elements, 1 member, last 42. |
| `bad_record_element_member_context`, `bad_record_container_event_nba`, `bad_record_element_member_ref` | A member of a container record element is staged only around assignment, call and system-task statements, so an `if` condition naming it rejects; an event-controlled write of a record with a queue member (the detached process has no frame storage for the queue copied at issue); the staged copy cannot be the actual of a `ref` formal, which must alias its storage (SV 13.5.2). |
| `native_lifecycle` | §§7.2, 10.9, 13.3-13.5, 23.3.3. (1) `touch(a, 1)` works on a copy: `a.leaf.notes[1]` stays `y`, the result has `y*`, `id` 11, and the shared counter object counts 1. (2) A run-time index `k = 0` writes `b.leaf.notes[0] = z`; `a` keeps `x`; the real member is 0.50. (3) `split` copies `b.leaf` out and adds `id` to the inout total: `root z 11`. (4) The port stage appends `>` and doubles the weight: `root> 1.00 z y*`. (5) A later member write propagates: `w root>`. (6) Nested calls append twice and count twice: `z** 31 3`. |
| `native_lifecycle_containers` | SIM-007-A01; §§7.2, 7.10, 8.4, 10.9, 13.4, 23.3.3. | `bad_chandle_record_port` | Frontend diagnostic: chandles shall not be ports (§6.14), including as record members. |
| `block_records` | §§6.21, 7.2, 7.5, 7.8, 7.10, 10.9, 11.4.11, 13.3-13.5. Records with string, real, class-handle, chandle and container members declared in an `initial` block own their members like module records. (A) `b = a` copies every member by value except the handle, so the later `a.q[0] = 9` leaves `b.q[0]` at 3 while `a.h.v = 6` is seen through `b.h`: `y 2 3 in 2.50 6 1 e 7`. (B) `foreach` visits `a.q` = 9 4. (C) The inner strings and `arr[1]` match (1, 1) while the queues differ (`!=` 1); (D) after `b.q[0] = 9` they are equal. (E) Copying through the module record `m`: `mod 9`, and `m.q` keeps two elements. (F) A named pattern sets every member: `p`, `q[1]` = 2, `z`, `k["w"]` = 9, `a`, null handle, one byte, no `"x"` key. (G) `push_front(0)` and `delete(1)` leave 0 2; deleting `"w"` empties `k`. (R) A record with a queue member passes by value into a function, which sums 1 2 3 and grows only its own copy: `6 3`. (S) A record result built from a copy carries the pushed 4 and the renamed `x+` while the source keeps three elements. (H) A static block record initializes once before the processes start, reading `base` = 7; the automatic one at block entry: `init 7 auto 8`. (I) A task input copies the record and adds `n` (8) to the inout total 1: `auto 9`. (J) An output formal fills a block record: `out 42`. (K) A known-false condition selects `b`. (L) An unknown condition keeps the equal `n` (42) and gives the empty string for the differing `s` (§11.4.11, as for module records). (M) A run-time index into a member string array: `p R q`. (N, O) A tagged union with a string member binds `str`, then holds `I` = 5. (P, Q) A nonblocking write to a static block record publishes at the end of the time step: `[] 42`, then `nb 9`. |
| `block_record_lifetimes` | §§6.21, 7.8.6, 9.3.2, 9.4.2, 23.6. (A) In each loop iteration the static `st` keeps counting (1, 2, 3; `s`, `ss`, `sss`), keeps the handle created in the first iteration (`v` = 0) and grows its queue, while the automatic `au` starts from its uninitialized value each time: count 1, `a`, a new handle with `v` = i and one queue element. (B) An automatic record's associative member is empty at each entry and its default set by the previous iteration is gone: the read of key 5 gives 0 with the §7.8.6 warning on stderr. (C) The static `si` initializes once (`i`, 10, `'{1}`) and counts 11, 12 with 2 and 3 queue elements; the automatic `ai` is initialized at every entry: `j 21 3 5`. (D) An automatic record in a `fork ... join` branch is reset at each entry: 0, 1. (E) A static record in a named block of an `always @(posedge clk)` keeps counting over two edges (1, 2; `+`, `++`) while an automatic one restarts at 1. (I) Each `leaf` instance owns its record (`one 3` at time 13, `three 5` at time 15). (G) Each generate block owns its record (`0 g`, `1 g`). (H) A same-named record in another process is separate storage: `other 0`. (F) The named block's static record is read hierarchically after both edges: `++ 2`. |
| `bad_block_record_fork`, `bad_block_record_automatic_nba` | An automatic block record whose block can be re-entered while a `join_none` branch of an earlier entry still reads it is rejected at code generation (one storage per declaration); a nonblocking write to an automatic record is illegal (§§6.21, 10.4.2) and rejected by the frontend. |
| `block_natives` | §§6.16, 6.21, 8.4, 8.16, 9.4.2, 10.4.2, 11.4.5, 13.4, 13.5, 25.9. Strings, chandles, class handles and a virtual interface declared in a named `initial` block. (A) The static `st` initializes in the static schedule after the module string `g`: `G1`; `t.len()` is 2, `up` returns `AB`; `glen` (an `int` initialized from `g.len()`) is 1. (G) The conditional gives `no`, then `itoa(123)` gives `123`, `atoi() + 1` is 124 and the replication `XbcdXbcd`. | `block_native_lifetimes` | §§6.21, 9.3.2, 9.4.2, 13.4.2, 23.3. (A) Over three loop entries the static string and handle keep their values (`""`, `s`, `ss`; the handle created in the first entry), while the automatic string, handle and chandle restart empty or null at each entry. The automatic handles stay alive in `keep`: 3 objects, `v` 10 and 12. (B) The static initializer calls `next_name` once before the processes start (`n1`, `calls` = 1); the automatic initializer calls it at each entry: `n2` (2), `n3` (3). (C) In a `fork ... join` loop body the branch's automatic `own` restarts empty at each entry, and both branches append to the block's automatic `shared`, which restarts at each loop entry: `12` twice. (D) A `join_none` fork in a loop that does not read the block's automatic string is accepted: `t0`, `t1`, then both children print at time 3. (E) A fork that runs once keeps its own automatic declaration for its branch (time 5: `fork`), and a block that runs once keeps its automatic handle for a branch running after the block ends (time 6: 77); `done` at 7. (I) Each `leaf` instance owns its static string: `one!` at 8, `two!` at 9. (G) Each generate block owns its string: `g0` at 10, `g1` at 11. (F) The named block of `always @(posedge clk)` keeps accumulating its static string (`+`, `++`) while the automatic one restarts (`+` each edge); the static one is read hierarchically at 15: `++`. (H) A same-named string in another process is separate storage: `[]` at 16. |
| `bad_block_native_fork`, `bad_block_native_always_fork` | An automatic string in the declaration list of a `join_none` fork that runs again in a loop, and an automatic handle of an `always` block read by a `join_none` branch, can be live in two activations; one storage per declaration cannot hold both, so code generation rejects them (§§6.21, 9.3.2). |
| `record_member_defaults` | §§6.8, 7.2.2. A record declared without an initializer starts from its type's member defaults. (A) `x`, 3, 2.25; the nested `in_t` record's defaults `in`, 1.50, and its nested fixed record's `a` = 5, two-state `b` = 0, `c` = a and the undefaulted four-state `u` = x. (B) The default on member `over` wins over `fin_t`'s own defaults: 1 2 3 4; `arr` = 7 8; the string array member is empty, the handle default null, the queue empty. (C) Module initializers read the defaults: `dl` = `"x".len()` + 3 = 4, `cat` = `in!`. (D) `m2` keeps its own defaults when `m` changes: `changed 0 x 7`. (E) The static block record `sb` starts from the defaults once and keeps its changes (`sb 4` at the second entry); the automatic `ab` starts from the defaults at each entry. (I) Each `child` instance starts from the defaults and adds its `ID`: 4 at time 1, 5 at time 2. |
| `bad_record_member_default` | A member default whose value is a record with a string member has no captured constant (the frontend constant of an unpacked record is not representable here), so code generation rejects the type rather than leave the member uninitialized. |
| `record_initializers` | §§6.21, 7.2, 10.5, 10.9. Module records are initialized from any record source in the static schedule. (A) The pattern `a`: `a 1 ai 2 3 1.25`; `glen` = `"G".len()` = 1. (B) `b = a` copies: `a 1 ai`, one queue element, equal to `a`. (C) `c = mk(g, 4)` runs `mk` once with `g` = `G`: `G 4 G-in 8 4 5 0.50`, `calls` = 1. (D) A pattern with the whole sub-record `a.inner` and a queue item: `d ai 2`, 3 elements, last 9. (E) `sel` = 1 selects `c`: `G`, equal to `c`; `cs` reads `c` and `b` after their initializers: `G-in/a`. (F) The copies are independent: pushing to `a.q` gives 2 elements while `b.q` keeps 1. |
| `record_view_equality`, `bad_record_view_equality` | §§6.8, 7.2, 10.9, 11.4.5. Nested records and member arrays of records with string, real, handle or container leaves compare member-wise. (A) Equal nested records, `int` and string member arrays: 1 1 1; the record-array member `ia` has never-written four-state `q` members (x), so `==` is x; `!=` of equal records 0. (B) After the writes: the strings differ (0), the arrays differ (1, 1), `ia[1]` differs in its string so `ia` is 0, and `ia[0]` still compares x. (C) A standalone `in_t` against nested records: 1 0 0. (D) Member arrays with different bounds of equal extent compare by position: 1 1. (E) Real member arrays compare numerically and queue members element-wise: 1 1. (F) Equal strings and an X bit: `==`/`!=` are x, `===` 1, `!==` 0; (G) a differing string makes `==` 0 and `===` 0. (H) A pattern whose whole nested-record items read the destination swaps them: `o x`, and `a.other` equals `solo`. Equality of a nested record with an associative-array member is rejected at code generation. |
| `native_multidim` | §§7.4.5, 7.4.6, 7.6, 10.9.1, 11.4.5, 13.5, 20.7, 26.2. A multidimensional fixed array of strings, handles or native records is one fixed view whose cells are stored in declaration (row-major) order; `a[i][j]` addresses one cell and `a[i]` the run of cells of that row. (A) `foreach` fills `s[i][j]` = `s<i><j>`: `s00 s12 s01`; `t = s` copies, and a later write to `t[1][1]` leaves `s` alone (`s11 X`); `!=` then `==` compare all cells. (B) `row = s[1]` copies the row out (`s10 s11 s12`), `s[0] = row` copies it in (`s10 s12`); `s[k][k+1]` with k = 1 writes `s[1][2]`, and `s[k-1] = s[k]` copies row 1 to row 0: `dyn dyn`. (C) Nested patterns: row 0 positional, row 1 `default` (`abc zzz`); keyed rows and items: row 1 has `k` at index 2 and `-` elsewhere, row 0 takes the outer `default` for each cell: `ddd--k`. (D) A formal, an output formal, a function result and locals of the array type copy the whole array (`f00f01f02f10f11f12`; `lo` independent of `lg`: `x00 y x01 x11`); `swap` through a `ref` formal exchanges `[0][0]` and `[1][1]` of the automatic block array (`m11 m01 m10 m00`); the static block array keeps its initializer (`p q r t`). (E) Descending ranges `[3:2][1:0]`: `d30 d21`, `$left(d,1)` = 3, `$right(d,2)` = 0, `$size(d,2)` = 2. A three-dimensional row copy `s3[1][0] = s3[0][1]` gives `110 010 011`. Rows of a typedef row type pass to input formals by value (`rows_equal`: 0, 1), to an output formal written back into `tr[0]` (`o-0 o-2`) and an inout formal that appends `!` to `tr[k]` (`t10! t12!`); string methods on a cell: `T12! 4 d`. (F) Record cells: `m10 10 1.500000`; a copy is independent (`m01 chg`) and differs (`F3`); a function sums the `n` members: 0+1+10+11 = 22; a pattern write and `m[k][0].n++`: `pat 99 1.500000 11`; a row copy of records: `m10 m11`; `m[1][0]` (n = 11) differs from `c[1][0]` (n = 10), so `F7` is not printed. (G) Handle cells copy identities: `h[0][1].v` = 1, `get()` of `h[1][1]` = 3; a write through `g[1][1]` is seen through `h` (77, same object); after `h[0][0] = null` the arrays differ; the increments reach the shared objects: `3 3`. (H) `%p` prints a nested assignment pattern. Some simulators print the cells of a multidimensional array as one flat list; llg follows 21.2.1.7 L36402-36404 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "value as an assignment pattern which may include the use of index labels. The use of white space is imple- mentation dependent; however the output shall be a legal interpretation of the assignment pattern syntax (see 10.8)", and a flat list is not a legal pattern for a `[2][2]` array (10.9.1). (I) A package array is one copy: the write of `C` is seen through the package function, and `tbl[k][k]` with k = 1 reads `d`. (J) `%p` of a slice `row[1:2]`, an indexed slice `row[k+:2]` and a row `s3[1][k]` of a three-dimensional array print one-dimensional patterns: `'{"y", "z"}` twice and `'{"110", "111"}` (decision S07-D2 covers the nested form). |
| `native_multidim_invalid` | §7.4.6 L8235-8237 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "If an index expression is out of the address bounds or if any bit in the address is X or Z, then the index shall be invalid. The result of reading from an array with an invalid index shall return the default uninitialized value for the array element type. Writing to an array with an invalid index shall perform no operation." An index is checked against its own dimension: (1) an X bit in either index or k = 3 reads empty strings; (2) `m[1][0]` (1 is outside `[3:2]`) reads an empty string, while `m[k][0]` with k = 3 is valid: n = 3; (3) a handle read outside `[0:1]` is null (`h[1][1].v` = 5). (4) The writes through invalid indices change nothing: `s00 s10 s01 m`. (5) Reading the invalid row `s[3]` gives the row type's default, empty strings; (6) writing it does nothing. Some simulators stop the run at a read with an invalid index; llg follows the clause text. |
| `native_multidim_nba` | §§10.4.2, 9.4.5. Nonblocking writes read their sources when issued and commit in the NBA region. (1) At time 1 the element, record-element and row writes (`ns[k]`, k = 1) are not visible after `#0`: empty strings. (2) At time 2 they are: `e xyz nb 4`, and the whole-array pattern and row copy issued at time 2 are not yet visible. (3) At time 3: `abc ddd`, and `nb[0]` copied `nb[1]` as it was at time 2: `nb 0`. (4) `ns[k-1] <= ns[k]` copies `ddd` and `ns[k][2] <= ns[0][0]` reads `a` at issue: `ddd dda`. |
| `bad_multidim_row_equality`, `bad_multidim_row_ref` | Equality of rows (§11.4.5) and a row as the actual of a `ref` array formal (§13.5.2) are legal; rows have no whole-array comparison and no aliasing view, so code generation rejects them explicitly. |
| `native_delayed_nba` | §§10.4.2, 9.4.5. An intra-assignment delay on a nonblocking write to a fixed array of strings, handles or records evaluates the source, the target position and the delay when the assignment runs (time 0: `src` = `a`, `k` = 1, `d` = 2; the later `src = "late"`, `k = 0` change nothing) and commits in the NBA region of the delayed step. (1) At time 1 nothing has committed: empty strings and a null handle. (2) At 2 the handle written at 1 is seen (`v` = 7); `mm[1][0]` commits at 2 after the display. (3) At 3: `mm[1][0]` = m, the record not yet. (4) At 4 the record: `r 2`. (5) At 5 the whole-array pattern of 4: `xyz`; (6) at 6 `ss[1]` = `a` of 5: `xaz`, the row of `mm[0]` commits at 6 after the display; (7) at 8 the slice of 7 and the row: `xst`, `pq`. |
| `record_element_member_contexts`, `bad_record_element_member_context` | §§7.5, 7.10, 12.4-12.7, 6.21, 9.2.2.2, 9.4.3, 9.4.5. A queue or dynamic-array member of a container record element read outside an assignment, call or system-task statement is read from a copy made before each evaluation. (1) `if`: the queue holds 3. (2) The `for` bound is read before every iteration: the push of 9 in the first iteration makes four iterations (1 2 3 9). (3) `foreach` over `fa[1].q` iterates the three elements and the body's writes reach the element: `10 20 30`. (4) Initializers: `m` = 4 and `fa[1].names[m-3]` = `y`. (5) The value of `n = #1 list[0].q[3]` is read before the delay: 9 at time 1. (6) The `while` condition sees each `delete`: one element, 1. (7) A `case` expression and (8) a string member in a condition: `three`, `x 3`. (9) `do ... while` stops at the size 3. (10) A conditional operator: 3. (11) A method of a queue nested in a queue element in a condition and a `return`: 1+2+3 = 6. (12) `always_comb` re-evaluates after the push into `fa[0].q`: 1. (13) `wait` on the member's size wakes at time 4 when the other branch pushes 8. Some simulators do not re-evaluate `always_comb` after a change to a container member of a record element (`c` stays 0); llg follows 9.2.2.2.1 L11184-11185 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "The implicit sensitivity list of an always_comb includes the expansions of the longest static prefix of each variable or select expression that is read within the block". An `if` condition that changes the member (`pop_back`) would change only the copy and is rejected. |
| `native_member_select_nested` | §§7.2, 7.4.6, 11.5.1. A run-time index into an array of records nested in a native record selects one member of the element (`m.e[k].s`): (1) k = 1 reads `e1`, `m.e[k+1].n` = 20 and the real member 0.5 equals 0.5: 1; (2) writes through `m.e[k].s` and `m.e[k+2].n` reach elements 1 and 3: `W 77`. An index with side effects is evaluated once: (3) `m.a[next()]` with k = 0 reads `a1` and leaves k = 1; (4) the write `m.a[next()] = "Z"` stores into `a[2]`, k = 2. (5) In a function's record copy, `r.e[i].s` with i = 2 appends `+` (`e2+a1`) without changing `m`: `e2`. (6) k = 9 is outside `[0:3]`: the empty string, 0 and 0.0 (§7.4.6 L8235-8237: "The result of reading from an array with an invalid index shall return the default uninitialized value for the array element type"). Some simulators stop the run at that read; llg follows the clause text. |
| `record_element_events` | §9.4.2 L11767-11769 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "The value changes on nets and variables can be used as events to trigger the execution of a statement." A member of a record element is a value like any other. `@`, `posedge` and `wait` on `nb[1].n`, `pb[1].n` (a record of integral leaves), `nb[1].v[0]`, `nb[2].s`, the run-time element `nb[k].n`, `names[1]`, `nb[0].a[1]`, `q[0].n` and `aa["k"].s` fire on a value change of that member (a whole-element write included) and not on writes of other members or of the same value. Expected values confirmed on an industry-standard simulator; only one line order among processes woken in one slot is free, so the `nb[k]` process prints after `#0`. |
| `record_element_selects` | §§7.4.5, 11.5.1 L15743-15752. Blocking bit, part and indexed part selects of packed members of record elements read and write the selected bits with the member's declared range: descending, ascending (`logic [8:15]`), multidimensional packed, elements of member arrays and sub-record members; compound writes; two-dimensional, queue, dynamic and associative elements. Expected values confirmed on an industry-standard simulator. |
| `fixed_variable_slice_actuals` | §7.4.3 L8093: "Reading and writing a variable slice of the array, e.g., A[x+:c] = B[y+:c]"; §7.4.6 L8210: "The term slice refers to a selection of one or more contiguous elements of an array." `a[i+:w]` and `a[i-:w]` as by-value fixed-array actuals count elements, over ascending, descending and offset ranges and a row. An out-of-range position reads the element default (0 for `int`, X for `logic`, §7.4.6 L8235). Expected values confirmed on an industry-standard simulator. |
| `record_element_member_nba` | §10.4.2 L13070-13072 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "If variable_lvalue requires an evaluation, it shall be evaluated at the same time as the expression on the right-hand side." Decision S07-D4. (1) Every leaf kind of an element commits in the NBA region: the `$display` of the same step still prints `0 [] 0.0 1`. (2) `nb[k].n <= 11` fixes k = 1; the blocking whole-element write and `k = 2` do not move it: `11 [w] 0`. (3) Bit and part selects merge; `v[0]` takes the last write: `11000100`, `00000f00`. (4) `#1`, `#2`, `#3` commit after the active region of their step, so the prints of those steps show the old values and the next one shows 5. (5) A 2-D element and `nb[bump()]`, one call. (6) k = 7 writes nothing (§7.4.6 L8235). (7) Member and whole-element NBAs of one step commit in issue order (§4.6, §9.4.5): 5 then 2. (8) The same from a task. (9) A sub-record and member arrays read `src` at issue (`srcv`, not `changed`), also with `#2`. Every NBA here is rejected by some simulators (dynamic types as NBA targets); §10.4.2 bars only automatic targets, so the outputs are derived by hand. |
| `record_container_nba`, `record_container_nba_sources` | §10.4.2 L13070-13072; §6.21 L7007-7008 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "Automatic variables and members or elements of dynamic variables—class properties and dynamically sized variables—shall not be written with nonblocking, continuous, or procedural continuous assignments." The text bars members and elements of a queue, not a whole queue, so a record's queue, dynamic and associative members take nonblocking writes (decision S07-D5). (1) `n <= m` copies every member when it executes: pushing to `m` afterwards leaves `n` with one element; the `$display` of the issuing step still sees 0. (2) `o <= #2 n` commits two steps later with the size at issue. (3) A whole element and a whole queue member of a fixed-array element commit the value at issue, also over a blocking whole-element write (S07-D4). (4) The sources are a call result, a pattern, a conditional, whole members and a later write in the same step (`p.s`), which wins by issue order. Some simulators reject every nonblocking write to a dynamic type, so the outputs are derived by hand. |
| `record_member_selects` | §§7.2, 7.4.5, 11.5.1. Run-time indices below a record element and through nested member arrays (`nb[1].a[k]`, `nb[k].a[j]`, `m.e[k].a[j]`, `m.e[k].b[2]`, `m.e[k].b[j +: 2]`, `m.e[j].w[k][j]`), on packed, string, real and handle leaves, with descending and ascending bounds and a two-dimensional member array, on module records, fixed-array elements and subroutine records. A value is evaluated first, then the indices left to right, each once. Expected output confirmed on an industry-standard simulator. |
| `record_member_select_invalid` | §7.4.6 L8235-8237 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "If an index expression is out of the address bounds or if any bit in the address is X or Z, then the index shall be invalid. The result of reading from an array with an invalid index shall return the default uninitialized value for the array element type. Writing to an array with an invalid index shall perform no operation." Each read gives its default, each write leaves the array unchanged. S07-D1 applies the same rule; some simulators stop, so the output is derived by hand from this clause. |
| `record_member_select_nba` | §10.4.2 L13070-13072 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "If variable_lvalue requires an evaluation, it shall be evaluated at the same time as the expression on the right-hand side." Decision S07-D4. (1) Writes below an element through run-time indices commit in the NBA region at the position of the issue: `k = 0; j = 0` afterwards moves nothing, and the `$display` of the step prints `0 0 []`. (2) `#2` writes issued at 1 commit in the NBA region of 3, so the prints at 2 and 3 show `0 7`. (3) A blocking whole-element write in between leaves the queued `21`. (4) `nb[bump()].a[bump()]` calls twice in all. (5) An index out of range writes nothing (§7.4.6 L8235-8237). (6) The same on a static subroutine record. Some simulators reject these targets (dynamic types as NBA targets); §10.4.2 bars only automatic targets, so the output is derived by hand. |
| `native_compound_selects` | §11.4.1 L14479-14480 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "An assignment operator is semantically equivalent to a blocking assignment, with the exception that any left-hand index expression is only evaluated once."; §11.4.2. `+=`, `*=`, `<<=`, `^=`, `++` and `--` through a run-time index, on integer, real and packed members of module, subroutine and element records, as statements and with a value (`$display("%0d", r.a[k]++)`). `r.a[f(1)] += f(2)` calls each once, the index first. An index out of range writes nothing. Expected output confirmed on an industry-standard simulator. |
| `record_event_nba` | §9.4.5 L12123-12124 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "An intra-assignment delay or event control shall delay the assignment of the new value to the left-hand side, but the right-hand expression shall be evaluated before the delay, instead of after the delay."; L12140-12141: "If the repeat count literal, or signed variable holding the repeat count, is less than or equal to 0 at the time of evaluation, the assignment occurs as if there is no repeat construct."; §10.4.2 L13070-13072: "If variable_lvalue requires an evaluation, it shall be evaluated at the same time as the expression on the right-hand side." Decisions S07-D6, S14-D2, S14-D7. (1) Every leaf kind of an element, and members selected through run-time indices, take `k`, `j` and the values of the issue; after the event the writes are still queued in that step (`[]` at 1, also after `#0`) and visible at 2. (2) `repeat (2)` fires on the second event. (3) `repeat (0)` commits in the step of the issue. (4) Selector, value, count, once each. (5) A blocking whole-element write between issue and event leaves the queued write. (6) An index out of range writes nothing (§7.4.6 L8235-8237). (7) A whole record copies its leaves at issue, also with `repeat`. (8) A whole element and sub-records. Some simulators reject these targets, so the output is derived by hand. Plain array forms of (1)-(4) were confirmed on an industry-standard simulator. |
| `record_queue_members` | §7.2 L7649-7650, §7.10 L8975 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "A structure represents a collection of data types that can be referenced as a whole, or the individual data types that make up the structure can be referenced by name"; "A queue is a variable-size, ordered collection of homogeneous elements." A queue of records as a member of a module record element and of a fixed array of records, element member writes included. |
| `native_member_select_records` | §§7.2, 7.4.6 L8235, 8.4, 10.4.2. Below a run-time selected element of a record array nested in a native record: `m.e[k].h.v` reads and writes through the handle member; `m.e[k].inner` and `m.e[k]` copy as whole values into records and formals and take blocking and nonblocking writes; `m.e[k].a[1]` selects a member array element; the same on a subroutine record. An invalid index reads the type's default and writes nothing (S07-D1 applies the same rule; some simulators stop). The lines before the invalid-index section other than the nonblocking ones were confirmed on an industry-standard simulator. |
